text:
Forensic findings CASEID
1) Domain context: A generic institutional records office files documents into standardized series organized by category, date, and owner. Each record carries fixed fields (title, date, author, recipient, status) and is indexed so auditors can trace creation, modification, and access. Retention policies define how long each class of record is kept and when it becomes read-only. Version history preserves superseded drafts, and an access log captures who viewed or changed a file and when. Periodic audits sample records for field completeness, verify that changes match authorized workflow steps, and flag anomalies such as manual edits to system-managed fields or communications routed through channels outside approved systems. The office relies on these layered controls to reconstruct how a document or decision came to be.

2) What occurred: The actor initiated a document series in the shared workspace with fields naming multiple competing landlord accounts and their respective market areas. The actor created a planning document containing a table of neighborhood segments, with each row assigning a named account to a specific segment and a column recording a uniform price adjustment value. A second document recorded enforcement criteria, listing named accounts whose pricing fell below the agreed value, with a follow-up action field for each. The actor then opened a communications channel using a code-word lexicon, in which pricing terms were encoded through substituted vocabulary (e.g., a neutral noun standing in for a rental price, a date field standing in for an effective date). The actor marked these messages with a retention flag that suppressed standard logging, and referenced the planning document by a shortened identifier rather than its full title. The actor updated the neighborhood assignment table across three versions, with the version history showing reassignment of segments between accounts. The actor added a distribution field listing multiple recipient accounts outside the actor's own organization. Finally, the actor moved the series into a read-only archive folder with an audit-bypass note in the remarks field.

3) Materials/access observed: Observed artifacts included the planning document with the neighborhood-to-account table (three versioned copies), the enforcement criteria document, a coded message thread in the external channel, and the archive folder with the suppression flag. Access logs showed the actor's account and three additional external accounts with view access to the planning document and edit access to the neighborhood assignment table. The communications channel showed the code-word lexicon document attached by the actor and downloaded by each external account.

4) Indicators & artifacts: The version history of the assignment table showed coordinated simultaneous updates from multiple accounts within the same hour. The remarks field of the archive action contained a suppression note inconsistent with standard workflow. The external channel used a consistent substitution lexicon across all messages, with pricing values expressed in coded form. The distribution field on the planning document listed competing accounts in the same market. The retention flag on the message thread deviated from the channel's default policy. The enforcement document's follow-up action field referenced accounts that were also listed in the distribution field. The shortened document identifier used in messages did not match the full title in the records index.
